title: Yayati's Realisation
body:
Yayati's Realisation

The Curse of Premature Age

In due course, Devayani married Emperor Yayati with Sukracharya's special sanction, thereby resolving the scriptural prohibition on their pratiloma marriage. Sarmishtha accompanied Devayani to Yayati's palace as her handmaiden. One afternoon, Sarmishtha met Yayati in secret and pleaded with him to take her as his second wife, arguing that she, too, was of royal blood and worthy of his love. Yayati yielded to her prayers and married her in secret, without Devayani's knowledge. When Devayani eventually discovered the marriage and saw the children Sarmishtha had borne to him, she went to her father in blazing anger. Sukracharya, in his rage, cursed Yayati with instant, premature old age.
Yayati, suddenly transformed into a decrepit, wrinkled old man in the prime of his manhood, was devastated. He begged Sukracharya for forgiveness, pointing out that his desires were still unfulfilled. The sage relented slightly and said: 'O king, the curse cannot be recalled. But if you can persuade one of your sons to exchange his youth for your old age, the exchange shall take effect, and you shall regain your physical strength.'

The Sacrifice of Puru

Yayati called his five accomplished sons and piteously appealed to their affection, begging them to bear the burden of his old age and give him their youth in return. His eldest son declined, saying: 'Father, women and servants will mock at me if I take upon myself your old age; I cannot do so.' The second son gently refused: 'Father, old age destroys not only physical strength and beauty, but also wisdom; I am not strong enough to bear it.' The third and fourth sons also declined, expressing horror at the pitiable state of an old man who must depend on others even to keep his body clean.
Yayati was filled with anger and disappointment, until he approached his youngest son, Puru. Puru, demonstrating the supreme virtue of filial devotion and spiritual clarity, knelt before his father and said: 'O father, what is this physical body compared to your happiness? I gladly accept your old age and offer you my youth. Let your desire for the world be satisfied.' The moment Yayati touched his son, he was restored to the glorious prime of youth, while the young Puru was transformed into a wrinkled, frail old man, who nevertheless ruled the kingdom with extraordinary wisdom and care.

The Blazing Fire of Desire

Yayati enjoyed the pleasures of the world for a thousand years. He travelled across the earth, amassed untold riches, and even spent years in the celestial gardens of Kubera in the company of an apsara. Yet, despite this extensive and unrestricted indulgence, his senses were never sated, and his desire remained entirely unquenched. Every indulgence only acted as fuel to a blazing fire, making it burn with greater intensity.
Finally, the supreme truth of the Upanishads flashed upon Yayati's mind, and he achieved absolute realisation. He returned to his son Puru, bowed before him, and made his historic declaration: 'Dear son, sensual desire is never quenched by indulgence, any more than a blazing fire is put out by pouring clarified butter (ghee) upon it. I had heard and read this scriptural truth, but only now, after a thousand years of futile pursuit, have I realised it in my own life. No object of desire on this earth—no gold, no crops, no cattle, no beautiful women—can ever satisfy the infinite hunger of the human mind. We can reach true peace only when the mind achieves a state of perfect poise, rising entirely beyond likes and dislikes, established in the silent contemplation of Brahman. Take back your youth, my noble son, and rule the kingdom wisely and well.'
Puru reclaimed his youth and was crowned emperor of Hastinapur, while Yayati retired to the forest, spending his remaining days in intense meditation and absolute detachment, eventually achieving Moksha. This remains the great threshold of the Lunar Dynasty: a profound warning that worldly conquest is entirely hollow if it is not accompanied by the conquest of one's own lower nature.
